appellation_rule.boundary_summary: Located entirely within Napa County, California, encompassing all of Napa County except the area northeast of Putah Creek and Lake Berryessa.
appellation_rule.grape_source_rule: 85% minimum from the named viticultural area per 27 CFR 4.25a
appellation_rule.geographic_features: Narrow alluvial valley roughly 30 miles long and up to 5 miles wide, bordered by Mayacamas Mountains to the west and Vaca Mountains to the east. Diverse microclimates from cool southern Carneros to warm northern Calistoga.

appellation_insight.overview: Napa Valley runs thirty miles north from San Pablo Bay, a narrow corridor where Mediterranean climate meets diverse geology to create California's most scrutinized wine region. The valley floor's deep alluvial soils and the hillsides' volcanic and sedimentary complexity offer radically different expressions within a few miles. What started as a farming valley in the 1800s became the stage where California proved it could make wines that age and compete globally.
appellation_insight.soil: The valley floor sits on deep alluvial deposits—Bale loam and Yolo silt loam—that drain well but retain enough moisture for vigorous growth. The eastern hills rise on sedimentary Franciscan formations, while the western Mayacamas Mountains offer volcanic soils from ancient eruptions, including the iron-rich Hambright series. These hillside soils force vines to struggle, concentrating flavors and creating wines with more structure than their valley floor counterparts.

context.grape_flavor_profile: Blackcurrant (cassis) is the signature aroma — instantly recognizable and consistent across regions. Dark cherry, black plum, green bell pepper (when underripe), cedar, tobacco, graphite, and dark chocolate round out the profile. The thick skin produces firm, grippy tannins and deep color. Cool-climate Cabernet (Bordeaux, Coonawarra) tends toward more herbal, structured, and mineral wines. Warm-climate versions (Napa, Paso Robles, Stellenbosch) show riper, darker fruit with softer tannins and more sweetness. Oak aging adds vanilla, toast, and spice — most serious Cabernet sees significant new oak.

appellation_rule.grape_source_rule: 85% minimum from the named viticultural area per 27 CFR 4.25a
appellation_rule.geographic_features: Cool maritime climate; strong cold winds and fog from San Pablo Bay; flat to gently rolling low hills; significant diurnal temperature variation; one of California's coolest AVAs.

appellation_insight.overview: Los Carneros sits at the southern end of both Napa and Sonoma valleys, where cooling winds and fog from San Pablo Bay create one of California's most distinctive cool-climate zones. This shared appellation between two famous counties has carved out its own identity through Burgundian varieties that thrive in its maritime influence. The region's rolling hills and clay-heavy soils produce wines with a tension and elegance that sets them apart from their warmer valley neighbors.
appellation_insight.soil: The soils are predominantly clay-based Haire and Diablo series, formed from sedimentary bedrock that holds water well into the growing season. These heavy clays force vines to struggle, producing smaller berries with concentrated flavors while the water retention helps them survive the maritime winds. The rolling topography creates multiple exposures and drainage patterns that allow winemakers to craft wines with different expressions from the same varieties.

context.grape_flavor_profile: Citrus (lime, lemon, grapefruit), green apple, white peach, and a mineral character that varies dramatically by terroir — slate gives a flinty, smoky quality (Mosel), limestone gives a chalky, broader character (Alsace), volcanic soils add a smoky depth (Kaiserstuhl). The acidity is the defining structural feature: electric, bracing, and persistent. Sweetness levels range from completely dry (trocken/sec) through off-dry (halbtrocken/demi-sec) to richly sweet (Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese). At every sweetness level, the acid provides balance. With age, Riesling develops the distinctive petrol/kerosene note (TDN) that is its calling card — a love-it-or-hate-it marker.

appellation_rule.zone: Cuneo province — Barolo, Castiglione Falletto, Serralunga d'Alba (entire territory) + parts of Monforte, Novello, La Morra, Verduno, Grinzane Cavour, Diano d'Alba, Cherasco, Roddi. Zone delimited by DM 31 agosto 1933 GU 238 del 12 ottobre 1933.

appellation_insight.overview: Nebbiolo's greatest expression, made from vineyards across eleven communes in the Langhe hills southeast of Alba. Barolo is often called Italy's Burgundy — not for flavor similarity, but for the obsessive terroir mapping, the vineyard hierarchy (MGAs), and the way subtle geological differences between adjacent plots produce visibly different wines. The appellation requires a minimum 38 months of aging (18 in wood) before release, and Riserva extends that to 62 months.
appellation_insight.soil: The soil divide is the key to understanding Barolo. The western communes — La Morra, Barolo, and parts of Novello — sit on younger Tortonian-era calcareous marl (Sant'Agata Fossili formation), with more calcium carbonate and sand. These soils produce more aromatic, approachable, earlier-drinking wines. The eastern communes — Serralunga d'Alba, Monforte, and Castiglione Falletto — have older Helvetian sandstone and compacted Lequio Formation marl with more iron and manganese. These wines are more tannic, more austere, and need longer cellaring. The specific MGA (Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive) vineyard sites add another layer — Cannubi, Brunate, Rocche dell'Annunziata, Vigna Rionda each have documented personality.

context.grape_flavor_profile: Pale garnet to brick-orange even in youth — one of the most deceptive grapes visually, as the light color belies enormous tannin and structure. Rose petals and tar are the signature aromatics — instantly recognizable and unique to Nebbiolo. Red cherry, dried herbs, leather, tobacco, violets, and licorice form the aromatic core. With age: truffle, dried flowers, autumn leaves, and a haunting complexity. The tannins are firm, fine-grained, and persistent — they coat the mouth and need years to resolve. Acidity is high, contributing to both aging potential and food compatibility. The texture is paradoxical: powerful but never heavy, astringent in youth but ultimately silky.

appellation_insight.overview: A southern Rhône cru village at the foot of the Dentelles de Montmirail, producing powerful Grenache-based reds that offer serious quality at a fraction of Châteauneuf-du-Pape prices. Gigondas was elevated from Côtes du Rhône-Villages to its own appellation in 1971, and the jagged limestone peaks of the Dentelles behind the village create a distinctive microclimate and dramatic vineyard landscape.
appellation_insight.soil: Clay-limestone at lower elevations, transitioning to stony, rocky marl and decomposed limestone on the slopes of the Dentelles. The higher vineyards have thin, poor soils with significant rock content — the limestone scree forces roots deep. Some sandstone outcrops add diversity. The rocky soils retain daytime heat but the limestone bedrock contributes a mineral freshness that distinguishes Gigondas from flatter southern Rhône sites.

appellation_rule.boundary_summary: Located in portions of San Mateo, Santa Clara, and Santa Cruz Counties, California, on elevated terrain of the Santa Cruz Mountain range.
appellation_rule.grape_source_rule: 85% minimum from the named viticultural area per 27 CFR 4.25a
appellation_rule.geographic_features: Elevated ridgeline above marine fog layer; Pacific Ocean influence through mountain gaps; thin, well-drained soils on steep slopes; significant temperature variation between fog-influenced western slopes and warmer eastern slopes.

appellation_insight.overview: The Santa Cruz Mountains AVA stretches across the fog-cooled ridges and valleys between San Francisco Bay and the Pacific, where elevation and maritime influence create one of California's most complex winegrowing puzzles. Vineyards here perch anywhere from 400 to 3,000 feet, with the higher sites catching morning fog that burns off to reveal intense afternoon sun. This vertical maze of microclimates allows everything from ethereal Pinot Noir to structured Cabernet Sauvignon to thrive within miles of each other.
appellation_insight.soil: The mountains offer a geologist's dream of fractured shale, sandstone, and limestone from ancient seabed upheavals, often with iron-rich red soils that drain quickly after winter rains. Decomposed granite appears on some ridgetops, while creek bottoms hold deeper alluvial deposits. These thin, well-draining soils force vines to struggle, concentrating flavors and creating wines with distinctive mineral backbones.

appellation_rule.boundary_summary: Located in San Luis Obispo County, California, in the Edna Valley surrounded by the Santa Lucia and San Luis Ranges.
appellation_rule.grape_source_rule: 85% minimum from the named viticultural area per 27 CFR 4.25a
appellation_rule.geographic_features: Cold marine air and morning fog drawn in from Morro Bay through the Cuesta Grade gap; among California's coolest coastal valleys; well-drained alluvial and volcanic soils on the valley floor and surrounding slopes.

appellation_insight.overview: Edna Valley sits just south of San Luis Obispo, carved by ancient volcanic activity and positioned perfectly to catch the Pacific's cooling influence through the Pismo Gap. This narrow, east-west oriented valley funnels marine air directly from Pismo Beach inland, creating one of California's most reliable cool-climate zones. The combination of volcanic soils and persistent afternoon winds makes it a natural home for Burgundian varieties that struggle in warmer inland areas.
appellation_insight.soil: The valley floor sits on ancient volcanic ash and tuff from nearby extinct volcanoes, creating well-draining soils with excellent water retention properties. These Positas and Diablo clay loams are interspersed with patches of Salinas silty clay, providing the stress-inducing drainage that forces vines to dig deep. The volcanic parent material contributes distinctive mineral elements that show up clearly in the wines.

context.grape_flavor_profile: Ripe red and black fruit — strawberry, raspberry, cherry, plum — with warm spice (white pepper, cinnamon, anise), dried herbs (garrigue, lavender, thyme), and a sweet, generous mouthfeel. Typically high in alcohol (14-16%) with low to moderate tannin and moderate acidity. Old-vine Grenache, especially from sites with stony or sandy soils, develops deeper concentration and a savory, earthy complexity that transcends the easy fruit of younger vines. The grape's naturally pale color deepens when yields are kept low.

appellation_insight.overview: Stags Leap District sits in a sheltered pocket on the eastern floor of Napa Valley, where the Vaca Mountains create a natural amphitheater that traps warm air while allowing cooling breezes through a gap in the hills. This small AVA gained international attention after the 1976 Paris tasting, when Stag's Leap Wine Cellars' Cabernet Sauvignon bested top Bordeaux in blind tasting. The combination of volcanic soils, strategic elevation, and unique airflow creates Cabernets with a distinctive profile—powerful yet refined, with an almost silky texture that sets them apart from the broader valley floor.
appellation_insight.soil: The soils are predominantly volcanic in origin, formed from ancient Pleistocene eruptions, with well-drained rocky loams and red volcanic ash over fractured bedrock. These porous, mineral-rich soils force vines to dig deep, contributing to the concentration and complexity found in the wines. The eastern hillside vineyards sit on steeper slopes with more exposed rock and better drainage, while valley floor sites have deeper alluvial deposits mixed with the volcanic base.

context.name: Leston Shiraz

scores.tasting_note: “A little reductive at first, give this time in a decanter or a glass. It soon reveals a heady nose of plum and berry fruit, green peppercorn, mint and soft baking spices, backed by a slightly charred, oak-driven character, like the smoldering embers of a fire. The palate is surprisingly powerful, tightly would with muscular tannins. A granular texture, pronounced acidity, drying oak and a sweet and sour fruit flavor are all present, too. Drink now and over the next few years.”

appellation_rule.boundary_summary: Located in the South West Australia Zone, Western Australia. Encompasses sections of Shires of Busselton and Augusta Margaret River lying west of longitude 115°18'E. Includes Dunsborough, Yallingup, Cowaramup, Margaret River, and Augusta. GI region 2,137 km², stretching ~100 km north to south along southwestern cape of Australia.
appellation_rule.geographic_features: Maritime-influenced Mediterranean climate. Lowest mean annual temperature range (7.6°C) of any major Australian wine region. Annual rainfall ~1,160 mm, only ~200 mm in growing season (Oct–Apr). Elevations 0–231 m. Ancient, highly weathered soils: predominantly deep red gravelly loam with gravelly surface transitioning to clay subsoil at ~1 m depth.

scores.tasting_note: Highly appealing from the word go. All dark fruits and spice, savory with a little mint and nori in the mix. It’s supple and giving across the mid-weighted palate, pliable tannins and a freshness throughout.

A generous mix of kirsch, cassis and blackberry flavors is dense and dark, accented by notes of palo santo, tobacco and cardamom. The tannins are dense, and a grace note of malty Assam black tea lingers on the finish, with plenty of harmony and firming tannins.

appellation_rule.boundary_summary: Located at the northern end of San Pablo Bay, spanning portions of both Napa and Sonoma Counties, California.
appellation_rule.grape_source_rule: 85% minimum from the named viticultural area per 27 CFR 4.25a
appellation_rule.geographic_features: Cool maritime climate; strong cold winds and fog from San Pablo Bay; flat to gently rolling low hills; significant diurnal temperature variation; one of California's coolest AVAs.

appellation_insight.overview: Los Carneros sits at the southern end of both Napa and Sonoma valleys, where cooling winds and fog from San Pablo Bay create one of California's most distinctive cool-climate zones. This shared appellation between two famous counties has carved out its own identity through Burgundian varieties that thrive in its maritime influence. The region's rolling hills and clay-heavy soils produce wines with a tension and elegance that sets them apart from their warmer valley neighbors.
appellation_insight.soil: The soils are predominantly clay-based Haire and Diablo series, formed from sedimentary bedrock that holds water well into the growing season. These heavy clays force vines to struggle, producing smaller berries with concentrated flavors while the water retention helps them survive the maritime winds. The rolling topography creates multiple exposures and drainage patterns that allow winemakers to craft wines with different expressions from the same varieties.
